title: A month later - a lot of changes and a lot more to do
author: Old-Wolverine-4134
selftext:
I decided to change a lot of things in the past 2 weeks, so now we have the start of the story paved out. Mechanics in the same as before, but now with more objectives and more to come.

Yes, the animations are horrible still, I will work on them soon. The trailer shows some bugs also mostly in the speech bubbles.

The sea rose and the world went under. You wake on a beach beside a wrecked boat, with no memory of how you got there. All that’s left is one scrap of land and an old camp someone abandoned long ago.

The story is shaping like so: Light the cold fire with driftwood, salvage what you can from the wreck, and patch the old hut. On a nearby islet, an ancient whale-shaped altar holds three moss-covered cards. With them you can raise new land from the sea, tile by tile: forests, mountains with rivers, meadows to farm, beaches.

As the island grows, old things rise with it out of the deep. There are relics, pages from a keeper’s logbook, and a lighthouse that hasn’t burned in years. Light it again, and maybe someone out on the water will find their way to you.

Somewhere beyond the horizon, something very large is still moving through the sea.

replies.author: mermaidreefer
replies.body:
AAA is cooked because they’ve been shite at story for a long time and hade the keys to code with large dev teams. Now those of us with good stories and mechanics can now, more than ever, get those out.

In ways, AI is definitely sapping the heart and soul out of the arts.

In other ways? It’s revolutionizing them. AI is handing paintbrushes to people who have ideas and dreams and stories and guiding their hand to get it out into reality.

comments.author: H4mst4
comments.body:
Very nice idea and concept.  
Wonderful what solo devs can achieve now.  
Can you explain your workflow in a few words?

replies.author: Old-Wolverine-4134
replies.body: Nothing special really. Just a lot of patience and tokens. I do countless edits until i get what i want. If I don't get the result i am hoping for, i move on and try later with more ideas. Decided to use Meshy for few models because they turn up nice and easy. Other than that the hardest part is the storyplay and the goal of the game. I have a blueprint for it, but it most likely will change many times.

replies.author: H4mst4
replies.body: so you coordinate the project and AI is doing the work? what AIs do you use besides Meshy?

replies.author: Old-Wolverine-4134
replies.body: 99% claude. Graphics and concept art with chatgpt.

comments.author: UseThisOneWhenStoned
comments.body:
So I just started aigamedev a few days ago; can you just briefly what your workflow looks like to create this?

Im quickly realizing how much of my game is going to rely on having some good art and animations for it. Are you generating those, using free assets or buying them?

replies.author: Old-Wolverine-4134
replies.body: almost all is procedurally generated in Unity. Art and models actually not the hardest part. Story and gameplay for me are hardest and I am still far from a good version of it.

replies.author: UseThisOneWhenStoned
replies.body: Interesting. Yeah my next step is taking one of my prototypes and getting it in an actual engine. Do you like unity so far? I've only considered that and godot so far.

replies.author: Old-Wolverine-4134
replies.body: Liking it or not, actually I am more interested if Claude can easily work with it. I tested Unity, Unreal, Godot for the same project. Each has it's own pros and cons. But Unity I think offers (for now) better understanding model-engine with all the previews and testing in between. But again, I am no pro and still learning a lot of things.

comments.author: ETZEEA

How much manual or human intervention did it take you to get this far? Is it like 70% prompts and 30% manual editing or what?

replies.author: Old-Wolverine-4134
replies.body: 0 manual editing. I don't touch unity except to hit play and preview the game.

replies.author: ETZEEA
replies.body: You've done this for a month, much longer compared to most gamedev using AI only for prototyping or slop. Anything you've learned that you might want to share that you picked up during development? like maybe tips and tricks on utilizing the AI efficiently or other stuff?

replies.author: Old-Wolverine-4134
replies.body: Just tell it what you want. I communicate with it like I am the player and Claude makes the game (which is true). I see result, I give it notes. If i have an idea, I brainstorm it with Claude to give me pros and cons and better ways to do it. And almost nothing comes up right from the first try. I can spend the whole day just on a single detail until it gets it the way I imagined. Ofcourse if you have some gamedev or coding experience, I imagine you can do much much better.
